Bauhaus: A modernist design movement that emphasizes basic geometric shapes, functional layouts, and stark typography over ornament.
Risograph: A stencil-based printing process known for distinct paper textures, limited spot colors, and slightly misaligned layers.
non-autoregressive: A model architecture that outputs predictions all at once in a single pass instead of generating text token by token.
calibration: The degree to which an AI model's stated confidence score reflects the actual mathematical probability of being correct.
tracking pixel: A tiny snippet of code added to a website to log visitors' activity and report it back to an advertising platform.
SameSite cookie: A browser security setting that determines whether a stored cookie is sent along with requests coming from third-party sites.
open-weight: An AI model whose trained internal numbers are released for anyone to download and run locally, rather than being locked behind an API.
VAE: Variational Autoencoder, a component in image generation models that translates compressed mathematical representations back into visible pixels.
model weights: The mathematical parameters inside a trained neural network that define its behavior and knowledge.
distillation: Training a new AI model by feeding it the outputs and reasoning produced by an existing model.
Overton window: The range of ideas and policies considered acceptable to the mainstream public at a given time.
ALPR: Automated License Plate Recognition, a system that uses cameras and image processing to track vehicle plates.
progenitor cell: An early stem-like cell that is committed to dividing and differentiating into a specific type of mature tissue.
in vitro: Studies or biological processes carried out in laboratory glassware or culture dishes rather than inside a living organism.
hindbrain: The lower back region of the brain that coordinates motor controls and vital involuntary functions like breathing.
sandbox: An isolated digital container where untested or untrusted code can run safely without affecting the rest of the computer or network.
orchestrator: A tool that automates the scheduling, scaling, and networking of many computing jobs across a cluster of servers.
UUID: A universally unique identifier, used in Bluetooth communications to advertise specific services or hardware models to nearby devices.
web-seed: A regular web server link included inside a torrent, allowing users to download files even if no other peers are currently sharing them.
SHA-256: A cryptographic hashing algorithm that produces a unique fingerprint for a file, used to verify the data was not modified or corrupted.
abliterated: A method of modifying an AI model's internal weights to bypass safety filters and refusal behavior.
HBM: High Bandwidth Memory, a 3D-stacked DRAM design that provides extremely fast data transfer speeds for AI hardware.
Glass carrier: A rigid temporary glass backing that holds a silicon wafer flat so it will not warp or snap while being ground down.
DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory, the standard working memory used in computers, phones, and graphics cards.
mirror domain: An alternative web address that serves identical copies of a website, often used to bypass blocks or share network traffic.
Tetris effect: A psychological phenomenon where dedicating hours to an activity causes you to involuntarily see its patterns in everyday life and dreams.
doomscrolling: Compulsively scrolling through endless feeds of depressing or alarming news on a screen.
private equity: Investment funds that pool capital to buy privately held businesses or take public companies private, aiming to streamline operations and sell them later for a profit.
management services organization: A third-party business entity that handles administrative, non-clinical operations and billing for healthcare providers.
treble damages: A statutory remedy where a court awards a winning plaintiff up to three times the amount of actual financial damages suffered.
linear content: Traditional television programming that runs on a set broadcast schedule rather than on demand.
EULA: End-user license agreement, the legal contract between a software or service provider and the customer using it.
SPARC: A processor architecture created by Sun Microsystems for its workstations and enterprise servers.
Solaris: A Unix operating system developed by Sun Microsystems to run on SPARC and x86 computers.
x86: The standard family of computer processor designs that dominates modern personal computers and servers.
reinforcement learning: A machine learning training method where a model learns by taking actions and receiving rewards or penalties.
prompt caching: Reusing previously processed prompt data so an AI provider does not have to recompute identical text on every request.
jailbreak: A prompt designed to trick an AI model into bypassing its built-in safety rules and content filters.
motivated explanation: An explanation designed to show why a mathematical idea or definition was chosen in the first place, rather than just mechanically verifying that it works.
Lean: A programming language and proof assistant used by mathematicians to formally verify that mathematical proofs contain no logical errors.
futures: Financial contracts where a buyer agrees to purchase a specific amount of a good at a set price on a future date.
ADFGVX cipher: A World War I field cipher used by the German army that combines letter substitution on a grid with a column transposition step.
LoRA: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes the original model weights and trains a much smaller set of adapter weights.
Brier score: A metric that scores the accuracy of probabilistic forecasts, where lower values indicate more accurate and confident probabilities.
Gated DeltaNet: A linear recurrent attention layer used in hybrid models to process sequences efficiently without full quadratic attention.
cmudict: An open-source pronunciation dictionary for English that maps words to sequences of phonetic sounds.
trie: A tree-shaped data structure commonly used to store and quickly look up strings based on their prefixes.
LLM: A large language model, which is an AI system trained on vast amounts of text to predict and generate language.
pairing mode: A temporary state where a wireless device broadcasts a beacon so nearby phones or computers can discover and connect to it.
adventure games: A video game genre focused on exploration, storytelling, and solving inventory or dialogue puzzles rather than fast reflexes.
Lua: A lightweight, embeddable scripting language widely used by game developers to write game logic.
RTS: Real-time strategy, a video game genre where players build bases and command armies simultaneously rather than taking turns.
Elo: A mathematical rating system used to rank competitors or AI models based on head-to-head game results.
priors: Your existing assumptions or beliefs before taking new evidence into account.
failure mode: The specific way or predictable pattern in which a system or plan breaks down.
MCP: Model Context Protocol, an open standard created to let AI assistants connect to external tools, databases, and services.
context bloat: When an AI model's working memory fills up with schemas and system instructions, leaving less room to process the actual task.
thinking tokens: Hidden tokens generated during an AI's internal reasoning phase before it returns an answer.
inference regime: The specific serving configuration, hardware limits, and compute budget allocated to run an AI query.
CRT: Cathode Ray Tube, an older display technology that shot electron beams at phosphors on a glass screen, producing distinctive scanlines and slight color bleed.
Dithering: An artistic technique of placing alternating pixel patterns side by side to trick the eye into seeing new colors or smooth gradients on limited hardware.
Anti-aliasing: Smoothing jagged, stair-stepped pixel edges by placing pixels with intermediate color shades along high-contrast borders.
open weights: An AI model whose underlying trained parameters are made available for anyone to download and run directly.
activated parameters: The specific slice of a model's total neural network weights calculated during a given request.
Lean formalization: Translating mathematical proofs into code so a computer proof assistant can verify that every logical step is strictly correct.
Computer Algebra System: Software designed to manipulate mathematical equations symbolically rather than just calculating numeric answers.
micropayments: Very small financial transactions, often just a few cents or fractions of a cent.
gamification: Using game mechanics like points, badges, and streaks in ordinary tasks to motivate behavior.
allocator: A component in code responsible for requesting, assigning, and freeing blocks of computer memory.
destructor: A routine that runs automatically to clean up a variable's memory when it goes out of scope.
carbon capture: Technologies that trap carbon dioxide emissions at the source before they can enter the atmosphere.
particulate matter: Microscopic specks of solid or liquid material suspended in the air that can cause respiratory issues.
Memphis Design: A playful 1980s aesthetic characterised by bright clashing colours, squiggles, and bold geometric shapes.
System 1: Fast, reflex-style classification decisions, in contrast to slower, step-by-step reasoning.
zero-shot: The ability of an AI model to handle a task without being trained on specific examples of that task beforehand.
fine-tuning: Taking a pre-trained base model and training it further on specialized data to make it perform well on a specific job.
third-party cookie: A tracking file saved by an outside domain rather than the website you are actually visiting.
SameSite: A browser setting that controls whether a cookie can travel along with cross-site web requests.
Weights: The numerical values learned during training that define how an AI model processes input and generates text.
Exfiltration: The unauthorized transfer or theft of data from an internal system to an outside location.
Distillation: The process of training a new AI model using the generated answers of an existing, often larger model.
XKeyScore: A secret National Security Agency computer system used to search and analyze global internet communications.
checkpointing: Saving a program's current memory and progress to storage so it can freeze immediately and resume later.
Kubernetes: Popular open-source software used to deploy, scale, and manage fleets of containerized applications.
Bluetooth advertising: The wireless broadcasts that Bluetooth devices send out periodically to announce their presence to nearby gadgets.
magnet link: A web link that identifies files by their cryptographic hash rather than the server address hosting them.
web archiving: Preserving snapshots of public web pages so people can still view them if the original page changes or goes offline.
mirror: An exact duplicate of a website hosted under a different web address, often used to bypass blocks or reduce server load.
RSS: A simple format that lets you subscribe to updates from websites without needing social media or algorithms.
linear Content: Broadcast programming delivered on a scheduled timetable rather than streamed on demand.
token: A small chunk of text, like a word or piece of a word, that AI models process and charge for.
context: The window of text and code an AI model can read and keep in mind at one time.
Erdős problem: One of hundreds of open mathematical problems posed by mathematician Paul Erdős, many of which carry cash bounties.
board of trade: An organized formal exchange where commodities and financial contracts are traded.
ADFGVX: A World War I German cipher that converts letters into pairs of coordinates and then rearranges their order.
dictionary attack: A technique to break encrypted text or passwords by systematically trying every word in a large list.
procedural generation: Creating content like text, maps, or levels automatically with code instead of designing it by hand.
line editing: The process of tightening word choice, rhythm, and clarity across sentences rather than merely fixing typos.
vibecoded: Slang for software built quickly using AI prompts rather than traditional careful engineering.
adventure game: A video game focused on story, exploration, and solving puzzles rather than fast reflexes or combat.
Pareto frontier: The curve of best-in-class options where you cannot improve on one measure, like price, without worsening another, like speed.
bwapi: A popular programming interface used by developers to write software bots that can play StarCraft: Brood War.
Model Context Protocol: An open standard designed to help AI models connect to external tools and databases.
Context bloat: When an AI model's working memory fills up with too many tool definitions and instructions, hurting performance.
Scanlines: The horizontal lines traced across a CRT monitor by its electron beam, often leaving faint dark gaps in between.
Navier-Stokes: A famous set of equations describing fluid motion, forming one of the unsolved Millennium Prize problems in mathematics.
JSONPath: A query language used to search and extract values from JSON documents.
Allocator: Code that explicitly requests and frees blocks of computer memory for a program.
Destructor: A routine that runs automatically to clean up resources when a variable goes out of scope.
fine particulate matter: Microscopic airborne particles from combustion that can enter the lungs and bloodstream, causing severe health issues.
tag manager: A web tool that lets companies easily inject and manage marketing and tracking code on their websites.
data exfiltration: The unauthorized copying or transfer of sensitive data out of a secure computer system.
progenitor: An early stem-like cell that can divide and turn into a specific set of mature cell types.
neural ectoderm: The specific layer of early embryonic tissue that goes on to form the nervous system.
VPN: Software that routes your internet connection through an encrypted server elsewhere, hiding your real location from websites and network providers.
management services organizations: Companies that handle the administrative, non-clinical business tasks of a medical practice.
OpenSolaris: An open-source computer operating system project created by Sun Microsystems based on its enterprise Unix system, Solaris.
jailbreak resistance: How well an AI model prevents users from tricking it into bypassing safety rules or guardrails.
quantizing: Shrinking a model by storing its numbers with less precision so it fits on cheaper hardware.
Millennium Prize Problems: Seven famous, unsolved mathematics problems established in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute, each carrying a $1 million reward.
Fields Medal: A prestigious award given every four years to recognize outstanding mathematical achievement in researchers under 40.
decision model: An AI model designed to pick discrete categories or scores from text rather than generate open-ended sentences.
substitution cipher: An encryption technique where letters in the original text are replaced with other letters, numbers, or symbols.
pixelhunting: A frustrating mechanic in older adventure games where players must hover their cursor over tiny screen areas to discover interactive items.
updating priors: Revising your existing assumptions or beliefs as soon as you encounter new evidence or data.
CLI: A command-line interface, which lets users or programs interact with software by running text commands in a terminal.
dithering: Arranging tiny alternating patterns of pixels to fool the human eye into perceiving new colors or smooth gradients.
anti-aliasing: Blending pixels with intermediate shades along edges to soften harsh stairstep patterns.
dot pitch: The spacing between the tiny colored phosphor elements inside a display, where a smaller gap means a sharper picture.
JPL: The Jet Propulsion Laboratory, a NASA-funded research center that builds and manages robotic planetary missions.
biosignatures: Substances or elements that provide scientific evidence of past or present life.
CAS: Computer Algebra Systems, software designed to manipulate mathematical expressions and symbols rather than just crunch numbers.
double-free: A memory bug that happens when a program mistakenly tries to release the same chunk of allocated memory twice.
combinator: A functional programming pattern where small, self-contained functions are chained together to transform collections of data without explicit loops.
lathe: A machine tool that spins a piece of metal or wood against a stationary cutting blade to carve round, symmetrical shapes.
mill: A machine that uses a spinning cutting bit moving along multiple axes to carve shapes into a block of material.
CNC: Computer Numerical Control, a setup where software coordinates motors to move machine tools automatically instead of turning hand cranks.
continual learning: Training a model incrementally on a continuous stream of new data without retraining it from scratch.
mixture of experts: An architecture that divides a model into smaller specialized sub-networks, using only a subset for each input.
catastrophic forgetting: The tendency of neural networks to abruptly forget older knowledge when trained on new information.
PIP: A Performance Improvement Plan, which is a formal probationary period a company puts an underperforming worker on, usually right before firing them.
Peter principle: The management theory that people in a hierarchy keep getting promoted based on current success until they reach a role they are incompetent at.
abliteration: A technique that modifies an AI model's internal weights to remove refusal behaviors without retraining the model from scratch.
CVE: A standardized identifier assigned to a publicly known software security flaw.
KL divergence: A statistical score used to measure how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution.
Creative Commons: A family of free public copyright licenses that allow creators to let others copy, modify, and redistribute their creative work under specific conditions.
decompilation: The reverse-engineering process of converting compiled, machine-readable binary code back into human-readable source code.
Screen Time: Apple's built-in settings panel for tracking device usage and setting parental or app restrictions.
Little Snitch: A Mac application that monitors network traffic and alerts you whenever an app tries to connect to the internet.
ctid: A Postgres row identifier that points straight to the physical page and slot where data lives on disk.
postings list: A search engine's internal lookup list mapping a specific word to every document that contains it.
BM25: A widely used ranking formula that calculates how relevant a document is to a search query based on keyword frequency.
left-pad: A simple string-padding utility that became famous in 2016 when its removal from the npm registry broke builds across the JavaScript ecosystem.
mock: A fake version of an external service or API used in automated tests to avoid making real network requests.
RSA: An encryption system whose security relies on how hard it is to factor the product of two huge prime numbers.
CADO-NFS: An open-source software implementation of the number field sieve algorithm used for factoring large integers.
GNFS: The General Number Field Sieve, which is the most efficient known algorithm for factoring integers larger than 100 digits.
cold reading: A technique where someone uses broad, statistically probable guesses to give the illusion of knowing private details about a subject.
subjective validation: A cognitive bias where people perceive generic statements as deeply personal and accurate simply because they find meaning in them.
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, a tuning method where human raters score chatbot outputs to steer the model toward more helpful conversational replies.
Forer effect: The psychological phenomenon where individuals believe vague, universally true statements describe their unique personality.
EEPROM: A type of non-volatile memory on a circuit board that stores low-level firmware instructions and settings.
RMA: Short for Return Merchandise Authorization, the process of sending defective hardware back to the manufacturer for a replacement or refund.
SKU: Stock Keeping Unit, an identifier used by manufacturers to distinguish specific product models and configurations.
NDT test: A network diagnostic tool used to measure internet connection speed and performance.
OSI model: A conceptual framework that divides network communication into seven layers, from physical signals up to application software.
local inference: Running an AI model directly on your own hardware rather than sending your queries over the internet to cloud servers.
gravity: A parameter in the ranking formula that progressively decays an article's score as it ages so the front page keeps turning over.
voting ring: A coordinated group of users colluding to upvote each other's submissions and manipulate rank algorithms.
variable aperture: A physical mechanism in a lens that changes the size of the opening to control incoming light and the depth of field.
bokeh: The soft, out-of-focus blur produced in the background of a photograph.
pull request: A proposed set of code changes submitted for review before being merged into a project's main codebase.
LaTeX: A markup-based document formatting system widely used for academic and scientific papers.
token prefill: The initial step where an AI model reads and processes your entire prompt before starting to write.
unified memory: An architecture where the processor and graphics chip share the exact same pool of high-speed RAM.
embedding: A list of numbers that represents the meaning and context of a word in mathematical space.
self-attention: A mechanism that calculates how much focus a model should place on other words in a prompt when predicting the next word.
air traffic control (ATC): The service provided by ground-based personnel who coordinate aircraft movements safely through airspace and on runways.
failover: An automated or manual switch to a standby secondary system when the primary system fails.
steganography: The practice of hiding secret data inside ordinary-looking files like images or audio so nobody notices it is there.
EXIF: A standard metadata format that cameras and phones attach to photos to record capture settings, dates, and sometimes GPS locations.
frequency domain: A mathematical representation of audio or image data based on frequency components rather than raw pixels or time values.
CI: Continuous Integration, an automated pipeline that builds and tests code every time a developer opens or updates a pull request.
runner: A virtual machine or server responsible for executing the automated tasks in a CI pipeline.
sharding: Splitting a large suite of automated tests across multiple machines so they run in parallel rather than sequentially.
phoning home: When software automatically and quietly sends diagnostic or user data back to the vendor over the internet.
Asahi Linux: A community effort to port and run the Linux operating system on Apple Silicon hardware.
Pyodide: A distribution of the standard Python interpreter and core data science libraries compiled to run inside WebAssembly.
WSGI/ASGI: Standard Python interface specifications that let web servers pass incoming requests to web frameworks either synchronously or asynchronously.
cold start: The initial delay that occurs when a serverless system must boot up an execution environment from scratch to handle a request.
